label: provisional
paradigm: These criteria serve a buyer choosing what to purchase, new or pre-owned: an evidence-based, value-aware buyer who wants an informed view of history and context. They are one reasonable buyer's stance, not the only one, and this version is provisional: drafted from published sources, not yet compiled or ratified.

change_log.reason: Converted from the two-watch collection taxonomy page of 2026-11-14 (artifact 7yWxiKfWGM7Yq4Uf1qapMU): 6 wearer, 9 watch and 7 pair criteria and its 10 references, wording kept. Kinds and evidence classes were assigned in conversion; the page's sources are informed opinion, so no criterion is classed research or deductive. Wearer-layer 'must' means the input must be established before any watch is scored. All checks are judged: the page gives no spec threshold that holds for every wearer. One citation changed: the page cites European Watch Company (its ref 2) for 'value', but that guide has no value-per-price passage, so 'value' cites Hodinkee Japan instead, whose author calls his 38 mm, 100-hour pair a relative value proposition (the next cheapest such watch being the discontinued F.P. Journe Octa).

brief.quote: Think about a scenario where you could only have two watches in your actual collection. And that has to serve you every single day. There's no price limitations.
brief.speaker: Teddy Baldassarre

wearer.statement: List the occasions the wearer actually faces in a year and how often (the occasion matrix). A black-tie event once a year is a different requirement from weekly client meetings.
Lug-to-lug length must sit inside the top of the wrist, and case thickness decides whether it fits under a shirt cuff. Measure these instead of trusting the stated diameter.
Does the wearer swim, surf, dive, garden or do manual work? That sets the water-resistance floor and whether a leather strap will survive.
How often does the wearer cross time zones? Frequent travel makes a GMT complication earn its slot.
Would the wearer be happy to be known by this watch? Some enthusiasts want a watch that draws no questions; others want one that says something.
Decide whether one anchor piece takes most of the budget or the money is split evenly. With no price limit, as in the video, this drops out.

watch.statement: Where the watch sits from dress to tool. Read it from thickness, polish versus brushing, dial busyness, strap and metal. The black-tie end is specific: thin, plain time-only dial, black leather strap, ideally precious metal. Bracelets, rubber and nylon read as casual.

What it survives: water resistance against the wearer's activities (30 m splash, 50 m casual swimming, 100 m snorkelling and surfing, 200 m recreational scuba), screw-down crown, lume and legibility, scratch-resistant crystal. A dress watch should never get wet.

Comfort across a whole day: size and thickness for the wrist, weight, bracelet comfort and fine adjustment, and how easily the strap swaps. A watch taken off by mid-afternoon fails here, however fine it is.

Score each complication on use, not prestige: date (daily), GMT (travel), chronograph (timing things), perpetual calendar (rarely needs setting, but delicate). Overlapping complications across the pair count against it.

The cost of ownership day to day: accuracy, power reserve (does it survive a weekend off the wrist?), automatic or hand-wound, serviceability. A hand-wound watch or a calendar that stops and needs resetting puts friction on a daily watch.

Mechanical interest and craft: movement design and finishing, in-house work, innovation, dial craft. This is the 'interesting mechanics' enthusiasts value and the reason several experts pick a hand-finished piece as their second watch.
Purpose, heritage, timelessness: is the design built for a purpose with historical roots? Will it still look right in twenty years? Is it neutral enough to go anywhere without inviting questions?
Attachment: would the wearer save it from a fire? Does it mark something in their life? With only two watches, each one has to matter.
What the money buys: quality, finishing and engineering per unit of price. It drops out under a no-budget brief, but enthusiasts still credit a watch that over-delivers for its price.

pair.statement: Every occasion row the wearer faces has at least one watch that fits it. Count the rows left uncovered, weighted by how often they occur.
The redundancy audit: do the two differ in register, case size, dial colour, complications and strap? Two similar dark dials, two chronographs or two 40 mm steel bracelets are one watch twice.

Can each watch's presence be explained by the collection's logic, rather than by wanting it or finding a deal? Do they share values (era, design philosophy, mechanical interest) even while they look different?
Name the watch the wearer would keep if they lost the other. It should be the one that covers the most wear-days, and it sets the collection's centre of gravity.
One deliberate contrast: brand origin, movement type, era or register. If nothing contrasts, reconsider one slot.
Remove either watch. Does a real gap open, meaning a set of days or occasions the other cannot serve? If not, the second watch is not earning its place.
Each watch should suit a distinct kind of day, so the morning choice is easy and neither sits in a drawer. If the wearer would want a third watch, the pair has failed.

coherence.statement: Two watches can each score well and still fail as a pair; judge differentiation and the gap test on the pair, not on either watch.

A pair passes coverage when every occasion row the wearer faces has at least one watch marked fits. The matrix cells are the page author's synthesis of the cited dress-code and water-resistance guidance; no source scores watch types this way.
